title: Thinking Sociologically
description: The sociological imagination, why common sense misleads, and Ibn Khaldun's science of society

concepts.title: The Sociological Imagination
concepts.contentHtml:
Suppose you lose your job. It feels like the most personal thing in the world: your savings, your pride, your plans. In 1959 the American sociologist C. Wright Mills (1916–1962) argued that feelings like these are where sociology begins. His book The Sociological Imagination asked readers to see how their own lives are shaped by forces far beyond them.

Mills drew a line between two kinds of problem. Personal troubles belong to a person's character and immediate relationships, and can be dealt with there. Public issues belong to the structure of a whole society. If one person in a city of 100,000 is out of work, Mills wrote, that is a personal trouble, and it makes sense to look at that person's skills and opportunities. When millions are out of work at once, it is a public issue, and no individual's effort can solve it. The same pain can be both: the trouble is real, but its cause lies in the economy.

The sociological imagination is the habit of moving between those two levels, connecting biography, history and social structure. For Mills the aim was "to translate personal troubles into public issues, and public issues into the terms of their human meaning for a variety of individuals."1 It cuts both ways. Sociology does not dissolve people into statistics; it shows how large patterns land in particular lives.

Mills was also a sharp critic of his own discipline. He mocked "grand theorists" who built abstract systems, and researchers he saw as "mere technicians" piling up data without asking what it meant. Every founder you will meet in this course faced the same tension: how to be rigorous about society without losing sight of the people in it.

concepts.title: Common Sense on Trial
concepts.contentHtml:
A familiar complaint about sociology is that it tells you what you already knew. In 1949 the sociologist Paul Lazarsfeld answered it with a trick. He was reviewing the first volumes of The American Soldier, a vast study built from surveys of US troops in the Second World War, and he listed some of its findings:

  • Better educated men showed more psychoneurotic symptoms than less educated men.
  • Men from rural backgrounds were in better spirits during army life than men from cities.
  • Southern soldiers coped with the heat of the South Sea Islands better than Northern soldiers.

Each sounds obvious. Intellectuals are highly strung; farm boys are used to hardship; Southerners are used to heat. Then Lazarsfeld revealed that the surveys had found the opposite. Poorly educated soldiers were the more neurotic, and Southerners were no better than Northerners at adjusting to a tropical climate. Had he given the true results first, he pointed out, readers would have called those obvious too.

The lesson is about hindsight. Common sense can explain any result after the fact, which means it cannot tell you in advance which result is true. Sociology earns its keep by checking, and the classics you are about to meet each found a way to check:

  • Harriet Martineau wrote a manual on how to observe a foreign society (1838).
  • Karl Marx mined British government reports on factory conditions.
  • Émile Durkheim built an argument from official suicide statistics (1897).
  • W. E. B. Du Bois surveyed Black Philadelphia house by house (1896–97).
  • Max Weber compared the world's religions across centuries.

Every method has blind spots, and lesson 6 puts two famous claims back on trial.

concepts.title: Ibn Khaldun's Science of Society
concepts.contentHtml:
More than four centuries before anyone used the word "sociology", a North African scholar set out to build a science of society. Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) was born in Tunis into a scholarly family and lost his parents and many of his teachers to the Black Death. After a turbulent career at the courts of North Africa and Muslim Granada, he withdrew for over three years (1375–1378) to Qal'at Ibn Salamah, in what is now Algeria.1 There, in 1377, he completed the Muqaddimah ("Introduction") to his history of the world.

Historians before him had mostly recorded events. Ibn Khaldun wanted to explain them, so he proposed a new discipline, 'ilm al-'umran, the science of human civilisation. Its central contrast is between badawa, the rural and tribal life of the desert, and hadara, settled urban life. Its central force is 'asabiyya, usually translated "group feeling" or solidarity: the bond that makes people cohere, cooperate and then reach for political power.2

From these he built a cycle. Tough desert groups with strong 'asabiyya conquer cities and found dynasties. Then comfort does its work. The first generation keeps its desert hardness; the second moves from privation to luxury, and one man begins to claim all the glory; the third has forgotten desert life altogether. As a rule, he concluded, no dynasty lasts beyond the life span of three generations, and he reckoned a generation at forty years.3

Should you call him the first sociologist? Many scholars treat him as a forefather of history, sociology and political science. Be careful with the label, though. He worked within Muslim legal thought and Greek philosophy as Islamic scholars had developed it, and he held that religion could strengthen 'asabiyya, at times decisively. He is best read as a brilliant precursor whose question, what holds a group together and what makes it fall apart, the founders of the 19th century would ask again.

title: Founding a Science of Society
description: Comte's positivism, Harriet Martineau's method and Herbert Spencer's social evolution

concepts.title: Two Revolutions and a New Word
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociology was born from two upheavals. The French Revolution of 1789 tore down a monarchy and the power of an established church, and left a question hanging: what holds a society together once its old authorities have gone? The Industrial Revolution then pulled people from villages into factory towns, creating new classes, new wealth and new misery. Thinkers across Europe began to ask whether society could be studied as scientifically as nature.

The word came first. The French political writer Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès used "sociologie" around 1780 in a manuscript he never published. It was Auguste Comte (1798–1857) who launched it: he first used it in print in 1838,1 at the start of the fourth volume of his Course of Positive Philosophy. Comte had worked as secretary to the reformer Henri de Saint-Simon from 1817 until they broke in 1824, and he coined the word "altruism" too.

Comte's positivism rested on two laws:

  • The law of three stages: humanity passes through a theological stage, which explains events by supernatural agents;2 a metaphysical stage, which explains them by abstract forces; and a positive stage, which seeks laws through observation.
  • A classification of the sciences: moving from mathematics through the natural sciences to sociology, generality decreases and complexity increases. Sociology, the most complex, comes last and crowns the rest.

The second law has aged far better than the first. Comte's later career took a strange turn. After the death in 1846 of Clotilde de Vaux, whom he idolised, he founded a Religion of Humanity in 1849 and published a Positivist Calendar to go with it. Its motto survives in an unlikely place: Comte's "Order and Progress" is written across the flag of Brazil.3

concepts.title: Harriet Martineau: How to Observe
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1838, the year Comte first printed the word "sociology", a British writer published arguably the first manual of social research method. Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) had made her name explaining economics to ordinary readers, then toured the United States. Her Society in America (1837) compared the country's professed principles with its practice, and found its treatment of enslaved people and of women impossible to square with the belief that all are created equal.

Her How to Observe Morals and Manners (1838) told travellers how to study a foreign society without fooling themselves. Its core rule still holds: "The grand secret of wise inquiry into Morals and Manners is to begin with the study of THINGS, using the DISCOURSE OF PERSONS as a commentary upon them." Conversations with a few locals mislead, she warned; institutions and records are steadier evidence. So study the churches and the clergy, epitaphs, popular songs, the treatment of the guilty. She also insisted that an observer who judges a people by the standards of home learns nothing about them, an early statement of what is now called methodological relativism.

One chapter heading should make you sit up: Suicide. Martineau told her readers: "The practice of Suicide is worth the contemplation of a traveller, as affording some clear indications as to religious sentiment." That was 59 years before Émile Durkheim made suicide rates the subject of sociology's most famous study.

In 1853 she published a condensed English translation of Comte's six-volume work, and Comte personally approved of it. For a long time she was remembered mainly as his translator, discounted in a profession run by men. Recent scholarship has recovered her as a founder in her own right, and her case raises a question this course returns to in lesson 7: who gets counted in the canon, and why.

concepts.title: Herbert Spencer: Society as Organism
concepts.contentHtml:
Quick: who coined the phrase "survival of the fittest"? Not Charles Darwin. It was the English philosopher Herbert Spencer (1820–1903), who introduced it in the October 1864 instalment of his Principles of Biology as another way of saying "natural selection". Alfred Russel Wallace seized on it, and Darwin agreed it was an "excellent expression".1

Spencer's system rested on one grand law. Evolution, he argued, is "a change from an incoherent homogeneity to a coherent heterogeneity": simple, uniform things become complex and differentiated. Stars, species, minds and societies all obey it, for "this law of organic progress is the law of all progress." A society, on this view, is like an organism. As it grows, its parts specialise and come to depend on one another, as organs do.

Spencer also sorted societies into types. Militant societies are run by rigid hierarchy and command; industrial societies are held together by contract and exchange, and the state shrinks to protecting citizens against force and fraud at home and aggression abroad. That made him a hero to opponents of state intervention, and the historian Richard Hofstadter later branded his thought a "biological apology for laissez-faire". The label social Darwinist stuck. Many scholars now think it is a caricature: one authoritative account calls him "typically, though quite wrongly, considered a coarse social Darwinist", and stresses his theory of moral rights.2

Spencer's reputation in sociology has faded, but his questions have not. How does a society differentiate, and what holds the specialised parts together? Émile Durkheim answered both by arguing against Spencer, as you will see in lesson 4.

title: Karl Marx: Class, Conflict and Capital
description: Marx as a sociologist: how classes form, the evidence he used, and how his forecasts fared

concepts.title: Class, Structure and Agency
concepts.contentHtml:
The Marxism topic in this app covers Marx the philosopher: alienation, historical materialism and surplus value. Here you meet Karl Marx (1818–1883) the sociologist, whose central claim is that the way a society organises production shapes the rest of social life. History, he held, runs through a series of modes of production, each marked by struggle between classes. The Communist Manifesto (1848), written with Friedrich Engels, puts it in one line: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

For Marx a class is defined by its relation to the means of production. Under capitalism the bourgeoisie owns factories, land and capital; the proletariat owns only its capacity to work and must sell it for wages. Sharing a position does not automatically make a group act together, though. In The Poverty of Philosophy (1847) Marx described workers thrown by economic conditions into a common situation: "This mass is thus already a class as against capital, but not yet for itself."1 Only in struggle does it unite and constitute itself as a class for itself. Later writers shortened this to class in itself versus class for itself, and the gap between the two became one of sociology's great research questions.

Marx knew the gap could stay open. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852) he explained why France's millions of small peasants could not act as a class: living side by side without real ties, they formed a nation the way "potatoes in a sack form a sack of potatoes." The same book holds his most quoted sentence on structure and agency: "Men make their own history, but they do not make it as they please; they do not make it under self-selected circumstances, but under circumstances existing already, given and transmitted from the past."2

concepts.title: Marx's Evidence: Blue Books and a Questionnaire
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx is often pictured as a theorist spinning systems in a library. In fact much of Capital (volume 1, 1867) is built from official British evidence. In its preface he explained that England is used as the chief illustration in the development of his theoretical ideas, because England investigated itself.1 He praised its factory inspectors, "as free from partisanship and respect of persons" as anyone could hope to find, its medical reporters on public health and its commissioners of inquiry into the exploitation of women and children. Germans, he added, would be appalled at the state of things at home if their own governments inquired as thoroughly.

Late in life Marx tried to gather evidence of his own. On 20 April 1880 the French journal La Revue socialiste printed his workers' inquiry (enquête ouvrière), a questionnaire of one hundred questions for French workers to answer about their own jobs.2 Its preamble complained that no government, "whether monarchy or bourgeois republic", had ever ventured a serious inquiry into the French working class,3 and argued that workers alone can describe with full knowledge the misfortunes they suffer. The questions are concrete: how young the youngest child workers are, what safety measures guard the machinery, whether the employer has ever compensated workers hurt in accidents.

Notice what this shows about method. The questionnaire treats the people being studied as experts on their own conditions, anticipating what is now called participatory research. It also has the weaknesses of any survey sent out by an interested party: questions that lead the respondent, and answers only from those motivated enough to reply. Marx's empirical side matters for how you judge him. His theory made claims about the real world, and claims about the real world can be checked.

concepts.title: Marx's Forecasts on Trial
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx's sociology came with forecasts. The Manifesto declared that "Society as a whole is more and more splitting up into two great hostile camps", bourgeoisie and proletariat, with the lower strata of the middle class sinking gradually into the proletariat. Crises would deepen, and the workers of the advanced industrial countries would overthrow capitalism.

On their own terms, the forecasts have fared badly. The revolutions made in Marx's name came first in largely agrarian Russia, not in industrial Britain or Germany, and the middle did not vanish. Take recent US data. A Pew Research Center analysis of government figures found that 61% of Americans lived in middle-income households in 1971 and 51% in 2023.1 Over the same years the lower-income share rose from 27% to 30%, while the upper-income share rose from 11% to 19%.2 The middle has thinned, as a Marxist might expect, but more people left it upwards than downwards. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on Marx concedes that history since his day "does not obviously confirm" his claim that socialism was developing automatically inside capitalism.

Two cautions keep the verdict fair. First, Pew sorts people by income, while Marx defined class by ownership, so the test is indirect; defenders reply that most people still live by selling their labour, whatever they earn. Second, Marx's tools have outlived his forecasts. Asking how economic interests shape politics and ideas runs through modern research on inequality, and Max Weber's reply, which split inequality into class, status and party, comes in lesson 5.

A last myth-check. False consciousness, the idea that people absorb beliefs that serve their rulers, is usually pinned on Marx. The phrase comes from Engels, in a letter to Franz Mehring of 14 July 1893, ten years after Marx's death:3 ideology, Engels wrote, is a process carried out "consciously, indeed, but with a false consciousness."

title: Émile Durkheim: Social Facts and Solidarity
description: Social facts as things, mechanical and organic solidarity, and the argument of Suicide

concepts.title: Social Facts as Things
concepts.contentHtml:
Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) did more than anyone to make sociology a university subject. In 1887 the University of Bordeaux appointed him to teach social science and pedagogy, which let him give the first official sociology courses in France.1 In 1896 he founded the journal L'Année sociologique, and in 1902 he moved to a chair at the Sorbonne. The First World War destroyed his circle: it killed many of his most promising students, and in 1915 his son André died in combat. Durkheim died two years later.

His founding move was to give sociology its own object. A social fact is a way of acting, thinking or feeling that is external to the individual and exerts constraint on them. A legal code, a language, a monetary system, religious beliefs and ways of dressing are social facts: they existed before you were born, and you feel their force when you defy them. So are rates of marriage, birth and suicide. Each case is an individual act, but the rate belongs to the society.

His first rule in The Rules of Sociological Method (1895) was to treat social facts as things.2 He did not mean that society is a physical object. He meant that you should study it from the outside, as you would study nature, setting aside your preconceptions, because society is a reality in its own right that cannot be reduced to individual psychology.

His idea of constraint deepened over time. At first it meant sanctions: break the rules and others punish you. Later he stressed internalised moral authority, which makes you feel guilty before anyone notices, and finally the pull of symbols people love. That last strand led to The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), built on ethnographic reports of Aboriginal Australian totemism. When a group gathers for ritual it produces collective effervescence, a shared intensity in which the power of the group is felt as something sacred and lodged in objects, from totems to crosses. The Studying Religion topic covers his definition of religion; for sociology, the point is that the sacred is society felt from the inside.

concepts.title: Mechanical and Organic Solidarity
concepts.contentHtml:
Durkheim's doctoral thesis, The Division of Labour in Society (1893), took up the question the two revolutions had raised: as people become more and more different from one another, what holds them together?

His answer contrasts two kinds of cohesion. Under mechanical solidarity, typical of small, simple societies, people resemble each other. They do similar work and share the same beliefs, and the individual conscience is almost the same as the collective conscience. Under organic solidarity, typical of modern societies, people are bound by their differences. The farmer, the nurse and the software engineer cannot live without one another, much as the organs of a body are interdependent. Specialisation, which looked like a threat to community, turns out to be a new form of it. To track the shift, Durkheim used law as an index of a society's structure: the kind of rules a society enforces reveals the kind of bonds it has.

Here he took aim at Herbert Spencer, who pictured industrial society as a web of private contracts between self-interested individuals. Durkheim objected that contracts cannot hold a society together on their own, because every contract rests on rules nobody negotiated.1 These non-contractual elements of contract decide what may be contracted for at all (you cannot sign away your basic civil rights) and rule out coercion and fraud. Markets, in other words, run on a moral order they do not create.

When that order fails to keep pace with change, Durkheim saw a pathology he called anomie: a state of deregulation in which the traditional rules have lost their authority and nothing has yet replaced them. One surprise for anyone learning the terms by rote: soon after this book Durkheim stopped using "mechanical" and "organic" solidarity altogether,2 though his concern with how societies integrate and regulate their members ran through everything he wrote next.

concepts.title: Suicide: The Argument
concepts.contentHtml:
To prove that sociology could explain what psychology could not, Durkheim chose the most private act he could think of. Suicide (1897) set out to show that although each suicide seems a lonely, inward decision, suicide rates are explained by the conditions of membership in social groups. He worked from official statistics and looked for patterns that no single biography could explain.

The pattern he leaned on hardest was religion: Protestant populations had higher suicide rates than Catholic ones. He explained such patterns with two dimensions of group life, integration (how strongly a group binds its members) and regulation (how firmly it governs their desires). Too little or too much of either produces a type:

  • Egoistic: too little integration. Life loses its purpose when the bonds of church, family or community are weak.
  • Altruistic: too much integration, so the group's claims override the individual's life, as in his example of self-immolation by Buddhist zealots.
  • Anomic: too little regulation. A crisis or a sudden change of fortune leaves desires without limits, a "mal d'infini".
  • Fatalistic: too much regulation, among people whose futures are "pitilessly blocked". Durkheim relegated this type to a footnote.1

Why should Protestants die by suicide more often? Not because of doctrine: suicide was forbidden and viewed as sin in both churches. Durkheim argued instead that Protestantism encourages free inquiry and so binds believers less tightly into a community, while Catholicism holds them within a group. The finding became so famous that one later review said it had been accepted widely enough to be nominated as sociology's one law. In lesson 6 you will see whether that law survives modern tests, and whether Durkheim's data were as solid as he assumed.

title: Max Weber: Meaning, Religion and Power
description: Verstehen and ideal types, the Protestant ethic thesis, and Weber on authority and bureaucracy

concepts.title: Understanding Social Action
concepts.contentHtml:
Max Weber (1864–1920), born in Erfurt in Prussia, came at sociology from the opposite direction to Durkheim. People, he insisted, are not simply pushed by external facts; they act on meanings. What a social scientist seeks to understand is the subjective dimension of human conduct as it relates to others. His word for this was Verstehen, interpretive understanding: grasping why an action made sense to the person doing it, and then using that to explain causally what happened. He built every concept, from the market to the state, on the meanings individuals attach to their actions.

Take a simple case. A man swings an axe. Observation tells you what he is doing; Verstehen asks why. He may be earning a wage, chopping wood for his own fire or venting his rage. The same movement is three different social actions, and a sociology that skipped the question would explain nothing.

Weber's second tool was the ideal type. Real history is endlessly messy, so the researcher builds a deliberately exaggerated model. In his words, "an ideal type is formed by the one-sided accentuation of one or more points of view";1 it is a utopia that cannot be found anywhere in reality. "Bureaucracy", "charismatic leader" and "Protestant entrepreneur" are ideal types. No real office matches the bureaucracy type exactly, and that is the point: you measure a real case by how far it departs from the model.

Third, Weber demanded value freedom (Wertfreiheit). Your values may legitimately decide which questions you find worth asking, but once you are analysing, the evidence must decide. For Weber this was as much an ethical virtue as a rule of method, and it remains one of the most argued-over ideas in social science.2

concepts.title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Weber's most famous work began as two long essays of 1904–05, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. Its puzzle, as he later framed it, was what combination of circumstances had led to the fact that "in the West, and here only", cultural phenomena such as rational, disciplined capitalism had appeared. Other civilisations had trade, cities and money. Why did this restless, reinvesting form of economic life take hold first in western Europe?

Weber's answer pointed to religion, and above all to Calvinism. The doctrine of predestination held that God had already chosen who would be saved, and nothing a believer did could change it. That, Weber argued, amplified believers' innermost anxiety about their own salvation.1 Puritan pastors of the 17th century answered it with practical advice: labour steadily in your calling, your worldly occupation, and read success there as a possible sign that you are among the elect. Combined with suspicion of enjoying wealth, this produced what Weber called inner-worldly asceticism: methodical work, with profits saved and reinvested rather than spent.

The twist is that nobody intended the result. The Puritans wanted salvation, not capitalism; the disciplined economy was an unintended consequence of religious ideas. Once established, capitalism no longer needed the religion. In the book's bleak final pages, the modern economic order has become an "iron cage" for everyone born into it. The English phrase comes from Talcott Parsons's translation; Weber's German, stahlhartes Gehäuse, means something closer to a casing as hard as steel.

Be careful what Weber did not claim. He did not say Protestantism caused capitalism on its own, and he did not simply reverse Marx by making ideas the only driver of history. He later wrote comparative studies of the religions of China and India to strengthen the argument indirectly. The thesis has been attacked from the start, and lesson 6 shows what happened when economic historians finally tested it with data.

concepts.title: Authority, Bureaucracy and the Iron Cage
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do people obey? Force alone is too costly; lasting power needs legitimacy, a belief that commands are rightful. Weber held that there are three types of domination that characterise authority relationships, each an ideal type:1

  • Traditional: the ruler is obeyed because it has always been so, bound by immemorial custom. Think of hereditary chiefs and monarchs.
  • Charismatic: followers obey because they believe the leader has extraordinary qualities, inspired by some transcendent power. Prophets and revolutionary leaders fit here.
  • Legal-rational: obedience is owed to a system of general rules and the offices they create. You obey the tax inspector because of the post, not the person.

Each type has a weak point. Charisma must keep proving itself, and a leader's excessive claims to miraculous powers, or followers' demands for proof, can destroy it. It rarely survives its bearer, so movements either fade or turn charisma into routine, with rules, successors and offices. This routinisation of charisma is one reason Weber expected legal-rational authority to spread.

Legal-rational authority works through bureaucracy: hierarchy, written rules, specialised offices and trained officials who act sine ira et studio, "without anger or passion". The Institutions and Law topic sets out his ideal type of bureaucracy in detail; here the point is his ambivalence. Bureaucracy is technically efficient and makes modern states and firms possible, yet it can reduce a person to a "cog in a machine". With science and capitalism it drives rationalisation, the calculable control of ever more of life, and the disenchantment of the world.

Weber split inequality the same many-sided way. Against Marx's single focus on economic class, he separated class (position in a market), status (social honour and way of life) and party (organised pursuit of power). In Weber's famous phrase, all three are phenomena of the distribution of power in a society.2 A noble family that has lost its money keeps status without class.

title: Classic Claims on Trial
description: How Durkheim's suicide statistics and Weber's Protestant ethic have fared under modern tests

concepts.title: Can Suicide Statistics Be Trusted?
concepts.contentHtml:
Durkheim treated official suicide figures as hard facts. Yet every number in them began as a judgement. Someone, usually a doctor, an official or a coroner, had to decide that a death was a suicide rather than an accident or an illness. If those judgements differ systematically between groups, the statistics measure the judges as well as the dead.

This is a live issue today. In England and Wales every suicide must be certified by a coroner and cannot be registered until an inquest is complete. Inquests take time, so only 39% of the suicides registered in 2023 had happened that year; 51% had happened in 2022 and the rest earlier.1 When the Office for National Statistics reported 6,069 suicides registered in 2023, a rate of 11.4 per 100,000 and the highest since 1999, the headline mixed deaths from several years.

For Durkheim's own era, the sharpest challenge came from the Netherlands. In 1996 Frans van Poppel and Lincoln Day used Dutch death records for 1905 to 1910, broken down by religion and cause of death, to compare individuals rather than regions. Catholics had lower recorded suicide rates, as Durkheim would predict, but more of their deaths were filed as "sudden death" or as due to ill-defined or unspecified causes. Catholic families had strong reasons to hide a suicide, including the scandal of burial in unconsecrated ground. Van Poppel and Day concluded that the Catholic–Protestant gap was explicable entirely by this way of categorising deaths.

That was not the last word. In 1998 Miles Simpson replied in the same journal, asking whether van Poppel and Day had combined apples and oranges. A much larger Prussian study found no sign of suicides hidden as accidents: reported suicides and reported fatal accidents rose together rather than trading off. Either way the lesson stands. Official statistics are social products, and you have to study how they are made before you trust what they say.

concepts.title: Retesting Durkheim
concepts.contentHtml:
A second objection is about logic rather than data. Durkheim mostly compared areas: Protestant provinces and countries had higher suicide rates than Catholic ones. That does not prove that Protestant individuals were the ones dying. Perhaps Catholics living as a minority in Protestant regions had the highest rates of all. Inferring individual behaviour from group-level data in this way risks the ecological fallacy, and critics of the book's method pressed the point from the late 1950s.

In 2018 the economists Sascha Becker and Ludger Woessmann published the most ambitious retest yet. They built a dataset of 452 Prussian counties for 1816–21 and 1869–71, when almost everyone belonged to a church. To get at causation rather than correlation, they used an instrument. The Reformation spread outwards in rings from Martin Luther's town of Wittenberg, so a county's distance from Wittenberg predicts how Protestant it became, for historical reasons that have nothing to do with suicide. They checked county results against cross-tabulated data to rule out the ecological fallacy, and tested for misreporting, weather and mental illness.

Their verdict: Protestantism had a substantial positive effect on suicide. In 1869–71 the average county suicide rate was 13.0 per 100,000, and across the 452 counties the raw correlation between the Protestant share and the suicide rate was 0.66. Tests using historical church-attendance data suggested that Durkheim's sociological channel, weaker community cohesion, mattered more than theology. Modern individual data add a twist. In 1992 suicide rates in their data were higher among Protestants than Catholics but higher still among people with no religious affiliation, and by 2009 only the non-affiliated stood out.

Group differences of the kind Durkheim studied remain stark. In England and Wales in 2023 the suicide rate was 17.4 per 100,000 for males and 5.7 for females, and males accounted for around three-quarters of suicides, a pattern seen since the mid-1990s.1 Durkheim's data were shakier than he knew, and his religious gap fails one individual-level test yet passes a larger one. The debate is still open.

concepts.title: Was Weber Wrong?
concepts.contentHtml:
Weber's thesis implies a testable prediction: Protestant places should have grown richer than Catholic ones because their people worked in a different spirit. For most of the 20th century the argument was fought with texts and case studies. In the 21st, economic historians have fought it with data, and the results show how a famous correlation can survive while its explanation falls.

First, Sascha Becker and Ludger Woessmann asked "Was Weber Wrong?" in a paper published in 2009. Using county data from late 19th-century Prussia, again with distance from Wittenberg as an instrument, they confirmed that Protestant regions were richer. But Protestant regions were also better educated, because Protestant economies taught people to read the Bible. In an early version of the paper they found that Protestants' higher literacy could account for the whole gap in economic prosperity; the published version said most of it.1 The engine was human capital, not a work ethic.

Second, Davide Cantoni tested the thesis where the Reformation began, in the German lands of the Holy Roman Empire. Using population figures for 272 cities from 1300 to 1900 (city size is a common stand-in for prosperity before modern statistics), he found no effects of Protestantism on economic growth.2 The result held across many controls and instrumental-variable estimates.

Third, Jörg Spenkuch studied individuals in contemporary Germany (2017). He found no effect of Protestantism on hourly wages, but Protestants did appear to work longer hours than Catholics,3 and differences in values, rather than institutions or education, accounted for most of the effect. That is the nearest thing to a Weberian work ethic in modern data, though it concerns hours, not wealth.

So the popular version of Weber, that Protestant hard work made northern Europe rich, finds little support. Yet the studies keep his deepest point: religion reshaped economic life through channels nobody planned.

title: Widening the Canon: Simmel, Du Bois, Addams
description: Three founders kept at the edges: Simmel's forms, Du Bois's Philadelphia survey, Hull-House

concepts.title: Georg Simmel: Forms and the Metropolis
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades the classical canon had three names: Marx, Durkheim and Weber. This lesson's founders were kept at its edges, for different reasons. Georg Simmel (1858–1918), born in Berlin to parents of Jewish origin, was one of the most popular lecturers in the city, drawing students and Berlin's cultural elite alike. Yet it was 15 years before he even became a titular professor.1 His biographers point to latent anti-Semitism, doubts about sociology's academic standing and envy of his popularity. He won a full chair only in 1914, at the age of 56, in Strasbourg, and died there in 1918.

Simmel's sociology studied the forms of interaction rather than their contents. Conflict, competition, subordination and secrecy take similar shapes whether they occur in a family firm, a church or a state, so forms can be compared across very different settings. His analysis of how a group changes when a third person joins two is a starting point for network analysis.

His essay "The Metropolis and Mental Life" (1903) asked what the city does to the mind. The city bombards you with stimuli, and you defend yourself by becoming intellectual, calculating and reserved. "There is perhaps no psychic phenomenon which is so unconditionally reserved to the city as the blasé outlook," he wrote:2 an incapacity to react to new sensations with the energy they would seem to demand. Money deepens the effect, since it turns every quality into a quantity, and the city's dense dealings require calculability and punctuality, which Simmel linked to the general spread of pocket watches.

He also gave sociology the figure of the stranger (1908): the person who arrives and stays, near and far at once, like a trader who settles in a town without fully belonging. Because the stranger is not bound by local loyalties, he can judge with an outsider's objectivity. An English translation of the essay appeared in the Chicago textbook of Robert Park and Ernest Burgess in 1924, and this lesson's last concept shows where that Chicago tradition came from.

concepts.title: W. E. B. Du Bois and The Philadelphia Negro
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1896 the University of Pennsylvania hired a 28-year-old historian, W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), to study the Black population of Philadelphia's Seventh Ward. Du Bois had studied in Berlin from 1892, working closely with the economist Gustav von Schmoller, and in 1895 he had become the first Black person to earn a PhD from Harvard. Penn gave him a temporary post as an assistant lecturer and, when it ended, no place on its faculty.1

What he produced in fifteen months of fieldwork was one of the first great empirical studies in American sociology. The work began with a house-to-house canvass of the Seventh Ward, using six schedules (structured questionnaires) across its roughly nine thousand Black residents. They covered families, individuals, homes, streets and institutions, recording age, birthplace, literacy, occupation, earnings, rent and lodgers. Du Bois added city-wide statistics, history and maps, and even had the people entering half the ward's saloons counted between 8 and 10 o'clock one Saturday night in December 1897: 3,170 people, 1,586 of them Black and 1,584 white.

The book, The Philadelphia Negro (1899), treated the troubles of Black Philadelphia as "a plexus of social problems" with historical roots in slavery, not as products of race. He went on to edit the Atlanta University Studies (1898–1914), a series of empirical reports on Black life. In The Scholar Denied (2015) the sociologist Aldon Morris argues that the white sociological establishment of the day largely ignored this work, and that the neglect distorted the discipline's account of its own origins.

Recognition came very late. In February 2012, more than a century after his temporary post ended, Penn honoured him with an Honorary Emeritus Professorship of Sociology and Africana Studies. His ideas of double consciousness and the colour line belong to the Race and Ethnicity topic; here the point is method. Du Bois showed that careful measurement could be turned against prejudice.

concepts.title: Jane Addams, Hull-House and the Chicago School
concepts.contentHtml:
On 18 September 1889 Jane Addams (1860–1935) and her college friend Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull-House in Chicago, a settlement house where educated residents lived among poor immigrant families. Three years later, in 1892, Albion Small was chosen to found a department of sociology at the new University of Chicago,1 and in 1895 he founded the American Journal of Sociology.

That same year Hull-House residents published Hull-House Maps and Papers. It grew out of a federal investigation: in spring 1893 the US Department of Labor, by order of Congress, surveyed the slums of great cities, and Florence Kelley, the agent in charge in Chicago, lived at Hull-House while she ran it.2 The residents turned the survey schedules into maps showing, house by house, the nationality of each household and the wages it earned across a third of a square mile, openly encouraged by Charles Booth's maps of London. Scholars now read the book as an early feminist method for studying urban inequality.3

The Chicago scholars, among them John Dewey, George Herbert Mead and Robert Park, worked in close exchange with Hull-House. Addams taught extension courses for the university for a decade but refused offers to join its faculty. In the following decades Park and Burgess made Chicago famous for a detached, scientific study of the city, including the concentric zones of The City (1925), and that sociology defined itself against social reform. As sociology, philosophy and social work split into separate professions, Addams was filed under social work, and her part in the other two was largely forgotten.

Addams won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931. Put this lesson's three figures side by side and a pattern appears: Simmel held back by anti-Semitism, Du Bois working in a segregated profession, Addams on the wrong side of a line drawn between science and reform. The canon is itself a social fact, and sociologists now study how it was made.
